newsitem.title: UK: Mexico debt move another good sign for investors.
newsitem.headline: Mexico debt move another good sign for investors.

text.p: Mexico's early repayment of loans which helped rescue it from the 1994 peso crisis is one more positive sign for investors and increases the chances the government may tap international financial markets again soon, London-based analysts said on Thursday.

The payment to the U.S. and the International Monetary Fund covers part of an almost $50 billion international package hurriedly put together when Mexico's economic crisis looked as though it would wreak havoc on the world's financial markets.
"It is obviously a good move...It adds further fuel to the fire (for booming emerging debt markets)," said West Merchant Bank economic adviser Peter West.
The initial impact on Mexican Brady bonds was fairly muted but traders said it added to the growing number of reasons to buy the debt.
It was bound to encourage new investors coming into the emerging debt market, tempted by the higher yields and its very quick recovery from the lows of early 1995 on the back of Mexico's problems.
The Brady bond market is currently at record highs.
Many in the market are increasingly bullish about Mexico which has so rapidly pulled away from near disaster, and are hoping for relatively strong growth this year.
Mexican par Brady bonds, currently standing at around 74 cents in the dollar, have risen close to two percent this month and are nearly 80 percent from the low hit after the peso crisis.
Analysts said there was no great concern that Mexico -- which is paying off the U.S./IMF debt early in part with longer-maturity loans borrowed commercially -- was simply putting off its problems.
West said the early repayment would in fact smooth out a hump in debt servicing due in 1998/99.
"Where this move will come into play is by strengthening the perception of Mexico's creditworthiness," ANZ emerging markets economist Chris Portman said.
"Mexico still has heavy external borrowing but this reassures the market that Mexico can deal with it," he added.
Analysts said the latest move will help Mexico look at tapping international financial markets again soon and possibly at another buy-back of its Brady bonds.
"I bet you there will be something else coming in the not too distant future," West said.
Of all the Bradys, the spreads on Mexican bonds are among those with the most room to tighten, analysts said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Stuart Parkinson noted that discount bonds now had a spread of 472 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, compred with 262 at their lowest in 1993.
"The cloud on the horizon is a political one," Parkinson added.
July sees mid-term Mexican congressional elections where the ruling PRI party is likely to face difficulties.
